heading: What the host does not do
body:
The host has no managed surface (a view that the host controls) for remote content. It has no always-on-top or opacity control beyond what the manifest grants. It has no global shortcut registry, and the page cannot show or hide the window, quit the app or change a tray icon. These features were once a fixed list of verbs compiled into each host. A fixed list limits what an application can do. If an application needs one of these features, it uses the feature from its service. It uses it in the language of the platform it runs on. A tray icon is the one exception: the manifest declares it in `tac.application.tray`, and the host builds it, like the menus (ADR 0107).

The host never shows another site inside the app. A link, a `location` change or `window.open` that leaves the app's own pages is cancelled. When it goes to an `http`, `https` or `mailto` address, the host hands it to the operating system, which opens it in the default browser or mail app. An `http` or `https` link must name a host and carry no user name or password. Every other scheme, such as `file:` or `javascript:`, opens nothing. This works the same on macOS, iOS, Android, Windows and Linux (ADR 0018).

The host also does not pass platform errors to the page. When a native service throws an error, the page gets only the fixed message "Native companion operation failed.", on every native host. The exception text stays in the app.
